claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure characterized by multilevel chemical fluctuations.
An integrated physics-informed machine-learning surrogate and multiscale fracture simulation can rapidly predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.
The surrogate can be trained on targeted ab initio and mesoscale cohesive-zone data.
The proposed framework couples a neural-network potential to cohesive-zone fracture simulations.
The framework is calibrated using selected experimental tensile and fracture-test data.
Microstructural heterogeneity governs local deformation in the hierarchical alloy.
Microstructural heterogeneity governs crack initiation and propagation in the hierarchical alloy.
A machine-learning surrogate can approximate expensive high-fidelity calculations more easily and rapidly than direct physical calculations.
The machine-learning surrogate can approximate mesoscale fracture behavior.
A cohesive-zone model captures crack-propagation dynamics in HfNbTiVAl10.
The integrated framework simulates elastic and inelastic responses more efficiently than direct ab initio or CALPHAD methods.
The proposed method will reduce computational time by approximately tenfold.
The proposed method will improve the prediction accuracy of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness by roughly 30% relative to first-principles or CALPHAD approaches.
Physically based mechanical-property predictions can require complicated and lengthy calculations.
Standard machine-learning approaches poorly predict fracture toughness in heterogeneous alloys of this type.
The method loses reliability when the tested microstructure differs substantially from microstructures represented in its training data.
The method loses reliability at loading rates outside its calibrated experimental range.
Prior literature supports the general efficiency and predictive utility of machine-learning surrogate models for alloy mechanical properties.
